usage_notes.narrative: Bergonzi prescribes playing modal scale sequences over a dominant sus4 chord specifically to remove avoid-note constraints, allowing the player to hear the pure sound of the key without harmonic interference. 'In the example below all of the notes are played over a dominant sus 4 chord. This allows you to hear the sound of the key without having to deal with any avoid notes.' Chapter 28, p. 113.

When rhythmizing scale sequences, Bergonzi directs the student to play the pattern starting from every degree of the scale modally over a sus4 chord, making it the recommended harmonic backdrop for systematic modal transposition practice. 'First play the pattern starting from every degree of the scale (in other words modally transposing it). In the example below all of the notes are played over a dominant sus 4 chord.' Chapter 28, p. 113.

For any chord quality approached by consecutive eighth-note groupings, Bergonzi's harmony anticipation rule prescribes that late displacement positions (#6, #7, #8 for a four-note group; #5, #6, #7 for five-note groups) automatically anticipate the next chord — either by approaching its notes, stating it directly, or letting the final eighth note sound the chord. 'For #6, #7, and #8, the harmony can be anticipated. That is, starting on the "and" of three, beat four or the "and" of four, you can anticipate the next chord by either approaching notes of the next chord or by simply sounding the next chord.' Chapter 3, p. 26.

When recasting any eighth-note line into triplet gear over a dominant (or any) context, Bergonzi prescribes leaving off either the first four or the last four notes of an eight-note phrase to make the line fit comfortably in triplet subdivision. 'To make this line feel comfortable in triplet gear you need to leave off the first four or the last four notes. In this case we'll leave off the last four.' Chapter 19, p. 83.

Bergonzi prescribes that in jazz playing, eighth notes over a dominant groove should coexist with the triplet feel rather than literally become triplets — sometimes by laying back or applying a lob. 'One way to improve your feel or placement of eighth notes is to notice how your eighth notes fit with the rhythm section which is often playing off of the triplet... your eighth notes should be able to coexist with the triplet feel... Sometimes this means laying back on the eighth notes or putting some type of lob on the notes.' Chapter 18, p. 77.

Bergonzi explicitly warns against playing eighth notes as literal triplets over a dominant groove: 'This doesn't mean that your eighth notes should be played as triplets like in this example, but rather that your eighth notes should be able to coexist with the triplet feel.' The feel is internalised, not mechanically applied. Chapter 18, p. 77.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing anticipating chord arrivals (including dominant arrivals) at offsets of 1/2 beat, 1 beat, 1½ beats, 2 beats, 2½ beats, and 3 beats as explicit rhythmic grammar rules. 'Anticipate chords by 1/2 beat, by 1 beat, by 1 1/2 beats, by 2 beats, by 2 1/2 beats, by 3 beats.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Over any chord change (including dominant resolutions), Bergonzi prescribes deliberately delaying resolution by 1 to 4 beats as a rhythmic grammar tool. 'Resolve late by 1 beat, 2 beats, 3 beats, or 4 beats.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Bergonzi's rhythmic grammar contains an absolute prohibition on starting or ending a phrase on beat one, applicable over all chord qualities. 'Never start on beat one. Never end on beat one.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Bergonzi prescribes that improvisers must alternate between passages that are predominantly eighth notes and passages that contain no eighth notes at all — avoiding the trap of relentless eighth-note density. 'Play predominantly eighth notes. Play without using eighth notes.' Chapter 29, p. 116; also Chapter 27, p. 110: 'Very often, less is more.'

At fast tempos over any chord, Bergonzi prescribes collapsing the felt pulse to 'two' or 'one' beat per measure to escape the eighth-note trap — the tendency to fill every subdivision. 'But if you want to get out of that zone for contrast try feeling the music in two or one. Try even perceiving a fast tune as a ballad.' Chapter 27, p. 111.

Bergonzi prescribes treating silence and phrase endings as active compositional events over any chord context: 'Leave periods at the ends of sentences and paragraphs. Know when to end your solo. Listen to the rests. The listener will invite your next idea.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Bergonzi prescribes playing solos using only half notes, quarter notes, and dotted quarters to create breathing room and enable rhythmic dialogue with the rhythm section. 'Try playing solos on any of the tunes using only half notes, quarter notes, and dotted quarters... Playing less notes at times allows the music to breath more. It also gives the rhythm section space for a little interaction and dialogue.' Chapter 27, p. 110.

Bergonzi prescribes first playing only accents through a tune (as if part of a horn section), then slowly filling in around those accents across several choruses. 'Try taking any tune and playing just accents as if you were the saxophone or trumpet section in a big band. After playing through several choruses, slowly fill in around the accents.' Chapter 27, p. 110.

Bergonzi prescribes developing awareness of which rhythms you are using and where you are in the bar, with the explicit rule that more notes per bar is not better than fewer — only different. 'More notes per bar is not better than a few, just different.' Chapter 1, p. 7.

Bergonzi prescribes treating consecutive note groupings as independent of bar lines — playing a fixed number of notes 'within and over the bar, or through the bar.' The groupings need not even be connected; internal mental grouping affects articulation even when invisible to the listener. Chapter 1, p. 9-10.

Bergonzi prescribes that a five-note grouping may be played over 1 beat, 1½ beats, 2 beats, 3 beats, or 4 beats — the same melodic cell flexibly rescaled to any duration over any harmonic context. 'The five notes can be played as 1 beat or 1 1/2 beats. 2 beats, 3 beats, or 4 beats, etc.' Chapter 1, p. 10.

Bergonzi prescribes displacing one-bar rhythms by 1/2 beat, 1½ beats, or 2½ beats to produce perceptually distinct rhythmic patterns over any chord quality. 'Notice that by displacing a rhythm 1/2 of a beat, or 1 1/2 beats, or 2 1/2 beats, you create entirely different sounding rhythms at times.' Chapter 2, p. 16.

Bergonzi prescribes superimposing odd-meter groupings (3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4, 11/4) over a 4/4 foundation as a systematic method for generating rhythmic variety over any harmonic context. The 5/4-over-4/4 cycle aligns on bar 6; the 7/4 cycle aligns on bar 8. 'This is a 3/4 pattern which takes three bars of 4/4 to work out.' Chapter 3, p. 27; alignment rules at Chapter 15, pp. 69, 71.

Bergonzi prescribes playing 3/4 rhythmic phrases over 4/4 tunes (hemiola) to ensure phrases begin from various beats rather than always landing on beat one, developing bar-line independence and horizontal playing. 'Practicing this rhythmic technique helps the improviser to become independent of bar lines and makes one's playing more horizontal... It takes four bars of 3/4 to equal three bars of 4/4.' Chapter 13, p. 63.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing hemiola (3/4 over 4/4) with a play-along while the right foot taps beat one and the left foot taps beat 3, combined with singing, to physically internalize the cross-rhythm. 'Try to practice these rhythms with a play along and also without a play along while your right foot taps beat one and your left foot taps beat 3. Also, try singing.' Chapter 13, p. 63.

Bergonzi prescribes converting consecutive eighth-note exercises into sixteenth-note (double-time) exercises by doubling up; the resulting 2/4 phrase is then repeated twice to fill a 4/4 bar. 'Take the material presented in Chapters 3-8 on consecutive eighth notes and convert them to sixteenth-note exercises by doubling up... repeat the 2/4 phrase twice to make a 4/4 bar.' Chapter 13, p. 62.

Bergonzi prescribes generating a 5/4 mirror rhythm (hemioval) by restating the same rhythm on beat 2-and that was started on beat 1, and a 7/4 mirror rhythm by restating on beat 3-and. 'By starting the same rhythm on beat 2 "and" that was started on beat 1, you get a 5/4 mirror rhythm.' Chapter 16, p. 72.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing explicit triplet rhythms on a tune and then switching to eighth notes on the same tune, in order to internalize the pocket through felt contrast. 'Practicing playing triplets is one way to get more connected to the rhythm section groove and so it can help to improve your placement of eighth notes. Try playing these triplet rhythms on Tune 8 (One Heart) and then play eighth notes to see if you feel a different pocket.' Chapter 18, p. 77.

Bergonzi prescribes expanding vocabulary by adapting any line to five distinct time zones or gears: quarter-note triplet, eighth-note, triplet, sixteenth-note, and sextuplet. These are interchangeable subdivisions deployable over any harmonic context. 'In this chapter we will consider five different time zones or gears to play in... The aim of this chapter is to expand your vocabulary by adapting lines to these varying time zones or gears.' Chapter 19, p. 82.

Bergonzi prescribes setting the metronome between 50 and 60 on the half note and repeating a line until triplets feel natural with eighth-note articulation. 'Set your metronome between 50 and 60 for the half note and play the line in its original form... Continue repeating the line until you are in the groove of triplets and phrasing them as if they were eighth notes.' Chapter 19, p. 83.

Bergonzi prescribes switching between time zones randomly and spontaneously during improvisation rather than programming gear changes, in order to develop transferable fluency. 'Rather than practicing this in a programmed fashion try using this technique randomly.' Chapter 20, p. 86.

Bergonzi prescribes a three-stage zone-mastery sequence: first go through the entire play-along track sticking to one time zone exclusively, master that zone, then master the next, then freely vary between zones. 'First go through the whole play-along track and try sticking to one time zone. Master that one and then go through and master the next, etc. Then try varying the zones moving from one gear to another.' Chapter 21, p. 88.

Bergonzi prescribes composing your own scale and intervallic sequences in a time zone as the benchmark of genuine mastery, not merely executing given exercises. 'Compose many other scale and intervallic sequences to really get the hang of it.' Chapter 21, p. 88; extended to 12 composed modal sequences over backing tracks in Chapter 28, p. 115.

Bergonzi prescribes internalizing 5-against-4 polyrhythm through repetition and articulation variation before moving to construction methods: 'Play this line or a line of your choice over and over again until you can feel the 5 against 4. Try using different articulations to enhance the sound of the line.' Chapter 22, p. 91.

Bergonzi prescribes building 9-against-4 by adding two notes to the end of an eighth-note line: 'Add one note to each bar of eighth notes or simply add two notes at the end of the original line to make nine notes per bar.' Chapter 22, p. 92.

Bergonzi prescribes building 10-against-4 by subtracting six notes from an eighth-note line, and 12-against-4 by subtracting four notes: 'Subtract six notes from the original line to make the ten notes... Subtract four notes from the original line.' Chapter 22, p. 92.

Bergonzi prescribes playing scale sequences in odd groupings of 5, 7, or 9 over any harmonic context: 'Another way to achieve similar results is to try playing scale sequences in 5, 7, or 9.' Nine-note sequences are played over four beats or two beats depending on tempo. Chapter 23, pp. 94-95.

Bergonzi prescribes that septuplets and nonuplets may be deployed over two, three, or four beats, selecting the metric span by context. 'You can try those septuplet rhythms over four beats, three beats, or two beats... Compose other broken nonuplets and play them over two, three, or four beats.' Chapter 23, pp. 102-103.

Bergonzi explicitly frames polyrhythmic mastery as a long-range pursuit, not a weekly drill: 'Becoming adept at playing all of these polyrhythms isn't a weekly pursuit but rather a long-range one.' Chapter 23, p. 100.

Bergonzi prescribes taking any fixed group of notes and reinterpreting it across different beat spans — from one beat through four beats, or compressed into 1½ beats — as a perceptual strategy for dissolving the strangeness of odd tuplets. 'Expand and try playing these five notes over three beats, and then over four beats. Next try playing the same five notes over 1 1/2 beats by contracting them.' Chapter 24, p. 106.

Bergonzi prescribes starting polyrhythmic exercises one beat early or one beat late so that the pattern crosses the 4/4 bar line, building polyrhythmic independence. 'If you need another challenge try moving all of the exercises over and starting them one beat early, or try one beat late, so that the polyrhythm goes over the 4/4 bar line.' Chapter 24, p. 105.

Bergonzi prescribes first isolating downbeat playing, then upbeat playing, then mixing the two on a single tune to develop fluid quarter-note soloing. 'Try playing just downbeats... Mix up downbeats and upbeats on this next tune.' Chapter 25, p. 107.

Bergonzi prescribes generating groups of seven by leaving out one note from two groups of four within a scale sequence. 'Leaving out one note in two groups of four creates groups of seven.' Chapter 28, p. 113.
Bergonzi prescribes adding rests within scale sequences as an active rhythmizing move: 'Leave out some notes and add rests.' Chapter 28, p. 114.

Bergonzi prescribes varying scale sequences by ascending or descending within them, and by skipping to any note in the scale to start the sequence: 'Ascend or descend within the sequence... Skip up or down to any note in the scale to start the sequence.' Chapter 28, p. 114.

Bergonzi prescribes a two-phase methodology for all sequence work: first familiarise yourself thoroughly with the sequence, then work through the possibilities with full creative freedom, composing 12 modal sequences and playing them over backing tracks. 'Start off with familiarizing yourself with the sequence and then work your way through the possibilities taking as many liberties as you'd like. Try composing 12 modal sequences and then playing each of them on one or more of the play along tracks.' Chapter 28, p. 115.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing without a metronome by meditating on a tempo, hearing quarter notes internally, then adding triplets or other rhythms mentally, with relaxation as the cognitive prerequisite. 'Internalize the rhythm section. Try to meditate on a tempo... Notice that when you become tranquil inside you then have a better perception of the time. Relax, above all, relax!' Chapter 27, p. 112.

Bergonzi prescribes varied metronome placements to develop time independence: on 2 and 4, on 1 and 3, on just 3, on just 4, or on the and of 2 and 4. 'Try using the metronome on 2 and 4, or 1 and 3, or just 3, or just 4, or on the and of 2 and 4.' Chapter 27, p. 111.

When practicing two consecutive eighth-note triplet groups, Bergonzi prescribes sounding only four of the six available subdivisions to develop rhythmic precision and selective articulation. 'Each one consists of two groupings of eighth-note triplets, but only four of the six notes are sounded.' Chapter 9, p. 47.

Bergonzi prescribes internalizing triplet groupings by playing a fixed four-note melody starting on different beats within triplet groupings before attempting free triplet improvisation. 'To get used to playing exercise #13, try playing the same four-note melody starting on the different beats.' Chapter 10, p. 49.

Bergonzi prescribes escalating from structured triplet-grouping drills to randomized practice as the final stage of mastery: 'Practice playing these preceding triplet groupings randomly.' Chapter 10, p. 50.

Bergonzi prescribes superimposing 4/4 one-bar rhythms (from the Chapter 2 palette of 22 rhythms) over a 3/4 harmonic context, and combining two 4/4 rhythms into longer polyrhythmic phrases over the 3/4 tune. 'Take any of the 22 one-bar rhythms in Chapter 2 and play them over this 3/4 tune. Next, try combining two of those 4/4 rhythms and play them over this tune.' Chapter 17, p. 74.

Bergonzi prescribes internalizing 3/4-over-4/4 polyrhythm by first practicing 3/4 rhythms exclusively, then combining any two to make a 6/4 cell, then combining four to create longer 3/4 lines over 4/4, and finally playing random 3/4-over-4/4 without any program. 'Try just playing random 3/4 over 4/4 using one 3/4 rhythm, then another and another without any program in mind. This really gets it into your unconscious mind.' Chapter 15, pp. 68-69.
